candidate.answerReason: A thinking student is a thinking human. A countermodel satisfying all premises can make statements (1), (3), and (4) false, so only statement (2) follows.

methods.label: Follow the thinking student and test the other claims
methods.explanation:
A logical consequence must hold in every arrangement satisfying I, II, and III. Use only the relationships stated in those premises.

By III, there is a student who thinks. By II, that same student is human. Thus some human thinks, proving statement (2).

To test the remaining statements, consider an arrangement with exactly two humans, Ada and Ben. Both are freshmen, Ada is the only student, and Ada is the only person who thinks. All three premises hold: every freshman is human, every student is human, and a student thinks.

In this arrangement, statement (1) is false because Ben is a freshman but is not a student. Statement (3) is false because Ada is a freshman who thinks. Statement (4) is false because the only thinking human, Ada, is a student. Therefore none of these three statements is forced by the premises.

Only statement \(\boxed{(2)}\) follows, so the answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
methods.levelReason: Tracking one existential witness and constructing a two-person counterexample require only elementary logical reasoning.
